raw_response.rationale: Full text read (14 pages, in Spanish). The study combines descriptive tabulation and GIS mapping of the 2009 CESPT residential water account registry (N = 495,684 active residential accounts in Tables 1-2; 346,979 mapped accounts in Map 2) with 34 semi-structured interviews (20 officials, 10 tanker-truck users in irregular settlements in Valle Redondo, 2 tanker operators, and 2 standpipe concessionaires). Substantively, the paper documents a rule-based tenure and tariff-regulation mechanism: CESPT requires legal land tenure for piped network connection, forcing irregular settlements to buy unregulated tanker ('pipa') water at $100/m3 versus $12.18-$12.19/m3 for formal metered users in 2010 (~8x higher, Table 3) and restricting irregular-settlement consumption to ~8 L/person/day versus 47 L/person/day among the lowest 50.63% of formal accounts. However, the empirical analysis is strictly descriptive and qualitative—reporting frequencies, percentages, group means, tariff schedules, and choropleth maps with zero inferential hypothesis tests, regressions, correlation coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals, test statistics, or p-values (uses of 'significativamente' and 'correlación' in the prose are purely colloquial). Flagging quantitative_synthesis_eligible = TRUE is therefore overstated.
